newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka eyes Iraqi crude in 1998.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka eyes Iraqi crude in 1998.

text.p: Sri Lanka might consider buying crude from Iraq next year if Baghdad is allowed to continue selling its oil, state oil firm Ceylon Petroleum Corp (CPC) said on Wednesday.
CPC Chairman Anil Obeyesekere told Reuters oil purchases from Iraq might be in return for tea, as suggested by some Sri Lankan tea officials in recent days.
His comments followed reports that Sri Lanka was preparing a high-level delegation, led by Trade Minister Kingsley Wickremaratne, to go to Baghdad soon to negotiate a possible deal.

Industry sources have suggested such a deal might make sense because Iraq already buys Sri Lankan tea via other countries in the Middle East and the Indian Ocean island needs to import all its oil requirements.
Obeyesekere said Sri Lanka used to buy around 300,000 tonnes of crude a year from Iraq, until Baghdad was barred from selling oil by the United Nations following the Gulf War in 1991.

Iraq is now allowed to sell up to $2 billion-worth of oil in return for humanitarian goods, including food, over 180-day periods. Baghdad is under pressure to sell oil quickly to comply with the strict terms of sale set out by the United Nations.
But Obeyesekere said there was no possibility of importing Iraqi oil this year because the country already had sufficient crude for its refineries under existing term contracts.

"It would not be this year," he said in an interview. "But maybe next year we would consider it because Iraq is a heavy purchaser of tea and to set off our balances maybe we (could) enter into some process whereby we trade tea for crude."
"We were importing about 300,000 tonnes of Iraqi crude so it could somewhere about that region. But of course we have not worked out our options," he added.
He said 300,000 tonnes of Iraqi crude could be worth about $35-$40 million.
Sri Lanka currently imports around two million tonnes of crude oil each year.
The Chairman of the Sri Lanka Tea Board, Clifford Ratwatte, said last week the island might negotiate a deal with Iraq similar to one agreed by India earlier this month.
Tea is Sri Lanka's biggest export earner and is expected to bring in around 35 billion rupees ($595 million) this year, after around 32 billion rupees in 1996.

Obeyesekere said the Sri Lankan government had given the go-ahead for possible Iraqi oil imports but no application had yet been made for such a deal to the United Nations, which oversees Iraq's oil-for-aid sales.

"At the moment Iraqi crude would not come into the country because we haven't applied for permission through the normal channels. But certainly next year this may be an option open to us if the sale of tea takes place."
